description: Creators, newsletters and podcasts reach the people you want, but the work around them is messy: a spreadsheet of names, pitches lost in inboxes, fees nobody adds up, and no idea which post brought sign-ups. This playbook sets up a Partnerships pipeline in the CRM, finds creators who already cover your space, drafts a personal pitch for each one you approve, gives every deal its own tracked link, and reports sign-ups and cost per deal, so you renew what works and drop what doesn't.

data.label: A mailbox to send pitches from

connections.label: An AI model, unless you run this from your own AI app

inputs.name: topics
inputs.label: What your buyers watch and read about
inputs.help: A few topics, so the agent looks for creators in the right places.

inputs.name: budget
inputs.label: Budget per partnership
inputs.help: Leave it empty to start with free product and commission deals only.

steps.say: Read the brand's context, and check its setup kit is applied so the Partnerships board and creator fields are there.
Look at partnerships already on the board, so nobody is pitched twice.

Find creators who already cover the topics, starting with people in your own records who create, then the web through your AI app. Add each one as a person with their platforms, audience size and topics, and a partnership at Found.
Vet each one (recent posts, audience fit, past sponsors) and move them to Vetted or Declined with a one-line reason.
Draft a short, personal pitch for each vetted creator as a sequence, held until a person approves the sends.
Watch for replies and move partnerships to Negotiating or Declined. For each agreed deal, make its own tracked link and promo code, save them on the partnership, and record the fee as spend.
When a post goes live, save its link and move it to Live; after two weeks, report visits, sign-ups and cost per sign-up for each, and move it to Measured.

guardrails: Never send a pitch, accept terms or promise money without a person's approval.
Only use contact details a creator publishes for business, and never contact anyone who opted out.
Ask every creator to label the post as sponsored the way their platform requires.
Stay within the budget per partnership, if one was given.

measure.how: Partnerships at Live or later on the board.
Sign-ups from each partnership's tracked link.
Each partnership's recorded spend divided by its sign-ups.

prompt: Run creator partnerships for {{brand}}. Their buyers follow creators, newsletters and podcasts about {{topics}}. Find ten creators who already cover this, vet them, and draft a personal pitch for the best five. Track every one on the Partnerships board, give each agreed deal its own tracked link, and keep each deal within {{budget}}. Nothing is sent or agreed until I approve it.
example: Northpeak sells trail running gear. The agent found twelve creators, three of them already Northpeak customers, vetted eight, and drafted five pitches. Two agreed: a newsletter for a flat fee and a YouTube channel for free product plus commission. After two weeks the newsletter brought 41 sign-ups at 12 USD each and was renewed.

title: Seed your product to creators
summary: Offer free product or credits to a vetted list of creators, give each a code and link, and follow up when they post.
description: Many creators will try a product for free and talk about it if they like it. Seeding costs little, but it only works if the list is right, the offer is clear and nobody is left without a follow-up. This playbook picks creators who fit, sends a short offer, gives everyone who accepts their own link and code, records what the product cost you, and checks back when they post.

data.label: A mailbox to send offers from

connections.label: Payments, to see which codes turn into paying customers
An AI model, unless you run this from your own AI app

inputs.name: offer
inputs.label: What you give
inputs.example: a free pair of trail shoes

steps.say: Read the brand's context, and check its setup kit is applied so the Partnerships board and creator fields are there.
Pick creators from the board at Found or Vetted who fit the offer, and suggest more from your own records who create, up to the number given.
Draft a short offer that says what they get and that there's no obligation to post, as a sequence held until a person approves it.

For each creator who accepts, set the deal type to free product, make their tracked link, save it and their promo code on the partnership, record what the product cost as spend, and move it to Agreed.
Two weeks later, check who posted, save the post link and move them to Live; suggest a friendly nudge for the rest.
After a month, report visits, sign-ups and paying customers per creator, and say who to offer a paid deal.

guardrails: Never send an offer or ship anything without a person's approval.
Never ask for a positive review or make posting a condition of the gift.
Ask every creator who posts to say they got the product free, the way their platform requires.

measure.how: Creators who posted divided by creators who accepted.
Paying customers from each creator's link and code.

prompt: Seed {{brand}}'s product to {{how_many}} creators. Offer {{offer}}, with no obligation to post. Pick creators who fit from the Partnerships board and our own records, give everyone who accepts their own link and code, and follow up when they post. Nothing is sent until I approve it.
example: Northpeak offered shoes to 20 creators. Fourteen accepted, nine posted within two weeks, and three of them brought more than 10 paying customers each. Those three were offered a paid video.

title: Split one data story by region for local journalists
summary: Turn one finding from your own data into a version per city or region, each pitched to the journalists who cover that place.
description: Local papers want local numbers. One dataset split by region becomes a story for every regional outlet, and each version has its own figures and its own journalists. This playbook makes one story per region from the brand's own aggregates, each with sourced facts and the expert's approved quote, and pitches each to the people who write about that place. A person approves every release and pitch.

data.label: A mailbox to send pitches from

connections.label: Geonode, so a news search per region finds local journalists
An AI model to draft the releases and write openers, unless you run this from your own AI app

inputs.name: finding
inputs.label: The finding
inputs.example: Share of small shops that block search bots

inputs.name: regions
inputs.label: The regions
inputs.help: Cities, regions or countries, separated by commas.

steps.say: Read the brand's context and experts, and save a news search for the topic in each region so local journalists are found.
Work out the finding for each region from the brand's own data, as aggregates only, and leave out regions with too few to be fair.
Start one story per region with its own facts and sources, and draft the expert's quote for approval.
Draft each release, check it and fix what the check finds. A person approves each one.
For each region, pick the journalists from that region's news search and a short sequence whose first step uses {{custom.opener}}.
Start the pitches, each waiting for a person, and report results by region.

guardrails: Never invents a number; a region with too little data is left out rather than guessed.
Uses the brand's data only as aggregates, never a figure about a person or a customer.
Every release and pitch waits for a person's approval.
A journalist gets one pitch a week at most, whichever region or brand.

measure.how: Coverage counted for each region's story within 30 days.
Articles that link to the brand's site, across the regions.

prompt: Run the "Regional data story" playbook for {{brand}}. Take this finding from our own data: {{finding}}. Work it out for each of {{regions}} as aggregates, leaving out any region with too little data. Make one story per region with its own sourced facts and a quote for our expert to approve, draft and check each release, then pitch each to the journalists who cover that region. Every release and pitch waits for my approval.
example: Northpeak split its bot-blocking finding across three cities. Leeds had too few sites and was left out; the Manchester and Bristol versions went to 9 local journalists and ran in 2 papers.

title: Sponsor newsletters and podcasts that pay back
summary: Shortlist newsletters and podcasts your buyers read, ask for rates, book small test slots, and scale the ones that bring paying customers.
description: Newsletter and podcast sponsorships are easy to buy and hard to judge. This playbook shortlists the ones that reach your buyers, compares them by price per 1,000 readers or listeners, books one small test slot at a time, and gives each slot its own tracked link and promo code, so the next decision is based on paying customers, not opens.

data.label: A mailbox to ask for rates from

connections.label: Web search, unless your AI app searches the web itself
An AI model, unless you run this from your own AI app

inputs.name: topics
inputs.label: What your buyers read and listen to

inputs.name: test_budget
inputs.label: Budget for the first test slots

steps.say: Read the brand's context, and check its setup kit is applied so the Partnerships board is there.
Look at partnerships already on the board, so nobody is asked twice.
Shortlist newsletters and podcasts on the topics, with their audience size and published prices, and work out the price per 1,000 readers or listeners where they share it.
Add each one as a company with its host or editor as a person, and a partnership at Found with the platform, deal type flat fee and the published price as the fee.
Draft a short rate card request to the best shortlisted ones that don't publish prices, as a sequence held until a person approves it.

Suggest which test slots to book within the budget, cheapest per reader first. For each slot a person books, make its tracked link, save it and the promo code on the partnership, and record the fee as spend.
Thirty days after each slot runs, report visits, sign-ups, paying customers and cost per paying customer, and say which to book again.

guardrails: Never book a slot, agree a price or pay anyone; a person does that from their own account.
Stay within the test budget.
Ask every newsletter and podcast to label the slot as sponsored.

measure.how: Each slot's recorded fee divided by paying customers from its link and code.
Partnerships that reach Renewed.

prompt: Find newsletters and podcasts about {{topics}} that {{brand}}'s buyers read and listen to. Shortlist them by price per 1,000 readers, ask the best ones for rates, and suggest test slots within {{test_budget}}. Track each slot on the Partnerships board with its own link and code, and tell me after 30 days which ones to book again. Nothing is booked or sent until I approve it.
example: Northpeak shortlisted 18 newsletters and 6 podcasts. Two test slots were booked for 1,300 USD in all. After 30 days the newsletter brought 9 paying customers at 44 USD each and the podcast 1 at 900 USD, so the newsletter was booked again and the podcast was dropped.

title: Take the links to your competitors' dead pages
summary: When a competitor deletes a page that others link to, show those sites what it said and offer your page instead.
description: When a competitor removes a page, every site that linked to it now has a broken link. Outflare notices pages gone from tracked competitors' sitemaps, reads who links to them, and keeps what the page said from the Internet Archive, so your pitch can offer a page that covers the same thing.

data.label: Your site added to SEO
A mailbox to send pitches from

connections.label: Ahrefs or DataForSEO, to read who links to a page (paid, within its budget)
An AI model to read pages and write openers, unless you run this from your own AI app

steps.say: List your competitors' pages that went dead and still have links, the most linking sites first.
For dead pages not read yet, read who links to them, after showing the cost and the budget.
Add the linking pages as competitor dead page prospects, with the dead page as evidence and your page that covers the same ground as the page to offer.
Check each new prospect's page with OutflareBot (free apart from the AI read) for whether it is up, already links, its broken links, what it is about and who to contact.
Pick a sequence for the pitches whose first step uses {{custom.opener}}, or create the starter sequence (a draft with the opener and one follow-up) if none does.
Start a pitch for each prospect worth asking, to its best contact. The workspace's AI writes an opener about their page, and each pitch waits for a person to approve it.
Report what was pitched and, later, what replied, agreed and went live.

guardrails: Never offers or agrees to pay for a link; a reply asking for money waits for a person.
Every pitch waits for a person's approval, unless they turned approval off for that sequence.
One pitch per website at a time, and never to a website that opted out or declined recently.
Every paid read shows its cost first and stays within the connection's budget.
Never criticises the competitor; the pitch is about the reader's broken link.

measure.how: Prospects from this playbook that reached Live within 60 days (Link building, Results tab).
Live links divided by pitches sent for this method, on the Results tab.

prompt: Run the "Take the links to your competitors' dead pages" playbook for {{site}}. List competitor pages that went dead and still have links, read who links to the best ones (show me the cost first), and add those pages as prospects with our closest page to offer. Check them and pitch each with an opener about the dead link and what it used to say. Every pitch waits for my approval.
example: A competitor of Northpeak deleted its sizing guide, which 41 sites linked to. Reading them cost 0.03 USD; 28 pages were still up with a contact, Northpeak's fitting guide was offered, and 6 switched.

title: Turn your own numbers into a story journalists want
summary: Find a surprising finding in your own data, write it up with sourced facts and approved quotes, and pitch it to journalists who cover the topic.
description: Journalists file stories built on new numbers, and a brand's own data holds findings nobody else can publish. This playbook looks for one in your data as aggregates, never about a person, writes the release with a source for every number and a quote your expert approved, and pitches it to the journalists who wrote about the topic recently. A person approves the release and every pitch.

data.label: A mailbox to send pitches from

connections.label: Geonode, so the news watch finds journalists who cover the topic
An AI model to suggest angles, draft the release and write openers, unless you run this from your own AI app

inputs.name: data
inputs.label: Where the numbers are
inputs.help: A saved query, a table or a report. Leave it empty and the agent looks through what Query can read.

steps.say: Read the brand's context and experts, and make sure a news search follows the topic so the journalists who cover it are known.
Look for a surprising finding in the brand's own data, as aggregates only, and suggest story ideas from it and the news.
Start the story, add every number as a fact with how to find it again, and draft a quote for the brand's expert to approve.
Draft the release from the facts and approved quotes, check it, and fix what the check finds. A person approves it.
Pick the journalists who wrote about the topic in the last two months, and a sequence of one email and at most one follow-up whose first step uses {{custom.opener}}.
Start a pitch to each journalist. The AI writes an opener from the story and their latest article, and each pitch waits for a person.
Report replies and the coverage that followed.

guardrails: Never invents a number, a quote or an expert; every number has a source and every quote the expert's approval.
Uses the brand's data only as aggregates, never a figure about a person or a customer.
The release and every pitch wait for a person's approval.
One email and at most one follow-up per journalist, stopping on any reply, and no journalist pitched twice in a week.

measure.how: Coverage counted for the story within 30 days (Stories, the story's results).
Articles that link to the brand's site, on the same results.
Journalists who replied divided by journalists pitched.

prompt: Run the "Data story" playbook for {{brand}} on {{topic}}. Look for a surprising finding in our own data ({{data}}), as aggregates only, and suggest the best angle. Write it up as a story with every number as a sourced fact and a quote for our expert to approve, draft the release and check it. Then pick the journalists who covered {{topic}} recently and start a pitch to each through a short sequence. The release and every pitch wait for my approval.
example: Northpeak's crawl data showed a third of the 1,200 sites it measured blocked their own customers' bots. The release went to 24 journalists who had written about bots that month; 3 asked for the data and 2 articles ran, one with a link.

title: Write content from your customers' questions
summary: Turn the questions people ask in replies into briefs for pages that answer them in search.
description: The questions prospects and customers ask by email are the same ones others type into search and AI assistants. This playbook collects them from the inbox, groups the ones that come up again and again, checks whether the site already answers them, and writes a short brief for each page that's missing.

data.label: Replies arriving in Outflare's inbox
Your site added to SEO

connections.label: An AI model, unless you run this from your own AI app

inputs.name: days
inputs.label: How far back to look, in days

steps.say: Read replies from the period and pull out every question.
Group questions that mean the same thing and count them.
Check which ones the site already answers and which pages target them.
Write a brief for each missing page and post them to the mission.

guardrails: Briefs never quote a customer by name or include their email address or company.

measure.how: Search Console clicks to pages written from the briefs.
How often the same questions arrive by email, before and after.

prompt: Run the "Content from customer questions" playbook. Read the replies from the last {{days}} days and pull out every question people ask about our product or problem. Group the ones that mean the same thing and count them. Check which ones our site already answers, then write a short brief for a page that answers each of the top five that it doesn't. Never quote anyone by name or include their email address or company.
example: Northpeak's inbox asked "can I export to CSV?" 23 times in 90 days and the site had no page about it. The brief became a docs page that now ranks first for "northpeak csv export".
